svg.title: Clearance decay as a measurement of effective dimension
svg.text: THE SLOPE OF THE CLEARANCE SEQUENCE MEASURES EFFECTIVE DIMENSION
11 400 insertions through this crate’s own solvers. Ground truth on the left, an unknown answer on the right
(a) Validation — farthest-first traversal, where the answer is known
Each series inserts a zero-radius point at the deepest spot, so dₖ is exactly the covering radius. The fits recover
2.10 for D = 2, but 3.53 for D = 3 and 4.93 for D = 4 — the estimator is itself short of its asymptotic regime.
(b) Application — the fractal distribution of example 01
Both series take the exact global maximum, so no search error enters. Both are clean power
laws (R² = 0.999 and 0.993) with exponents steeper than −0.5: the distributions occupy
less than the plane they are drawn in, and the two rules are cleanly distinguished.
A slope steeper than −1/2 in the plane is the signature of a fractal support.
as ff4, four times the restarts
Figure 5 | The diagnostic of §2.1, carried out. (a) Farthest-first traversal, where the covering radius must scale as k^(−1/D): the fit recovers
2.10 against a true 2, but only 3.53 against 3 and 4.93 against 4. The control row ff4hi isolates the cause — quadrupling the restarts moves the slope
further from −1/4, not closer, so the shortfall is not search error but the pre-asymptotic regime. Reaching k ≫ 2^D insertions is itself subject to the
curse of dimensionality, so the estimator inherits the very limitation it measures. (b) Applied where no ground truth exists, the same fit is far cleaner
(R² = 0.9993) and returns 1.89 for the distribution of example 01 and 1.21 for maximal balls — non-integer dimensions below the ambient 2, which is
what a fractal support should give. Shaded: clearances within 20 cells of the discrete solver’s grid pitch, excluded from every fit.
